title: Green Potatoes: Why They Turn Green and When Not to Eat Them

seo.title: Are Green Potatoes Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: Green color is chlorophyll, but light exposure can also increase potato glycoalkaloids. Learn why green potatoes are best discarded.
seo.search_intent: Food safety explanation of green potatoes.

excerpt: The green pigment itself is harmless chlorophyll, but greening signals light exposure that can also raise glycoalkaloids such as solanine and chaconine. EFSA's consumer guidance says green potatoes should not be eaten.
content_html:
A green potato has produced chlorophyll after light exposure. Chlorophyll is not the toxin. The concern is that the same stress can increase natural potato defense compounds called glycoalkaloids.

Green is a warning signal, not a glycoalkaloid meter

Greenness does not tell you an exact solanine concentration. Some non-green potatoes can contain glycoalkaloids too. But visible green tissue is a practical sign that storage conditions favored unwanted changes.

Should you just cut the green part away?

Peeling can reduce glycoalkaloids because they are concentrated near the skin. EFSA consumer guidance nonetheless advises not eating green potatoes. That avoids pretending a home cook can measure the starting concentration.

Cooking is not a reliable rescue method

EFSA reports broad reductions from peeling, boiling and frying, but the ranges are too variable to guarantee a particular green potato has been made safe.

Possible symptoms

High glycoalkaloid intake can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Bitter taste and oral burning can be warning signs, but do not taste-test a suspicious potato.

Prevent greening

Store potatoes cool, dry, ventilated and protected from light. Do not keep them for days in direct sunlight or under strong kitchen lights.

A quick decision guide

What you seeWhat it means in practice
Normal skin color, firm potatoUse normally if otherwise sound
Clearly green skin or fleshDiscard
Green plus many sprouts or shrivelingDiscard
Bitter taste or oral burningStop eating and discard

The green pigment is chlorophyll, not solanine. The reason green potatoes are treated cautiously is that light exposure can stimulate chlorophyll and glycoalkaloid formation at the same time.

Why green color cannot tell you the exact toxin level

Two potatoes with the same shade of green do not necessarily contain the same amount of glycoalkaloids. Variety, storage conditions, damage and the depth of the green tissue all matter. Conversely, a potato does not need to look intensely green to contain some glycoalkaloids.

That uncertainty is exactly why visible greening is used as a practical warning rather than as a home measurement. EFSA consumer guidance recommends not eating green potatoes instead of asking people to estimate a concentration from color.

How much do peeling and cooking reduce glycoalkaloids?

Processing can reduce them, but the range is wide. EFSA reports reductions of approximately 25–75% from peeling, 5–65% from boiling and 20–90% from frying in oil. A wide range means there is no reliable household calculation such as “boiling removes half, so this green potato is safe.”

For a normal, non-green potato, those processing effects are part of ordinary cooking. For a clearly green potato, they are not a good reason to override the simpler advice to discard it.

What does the 1 mg/kg figure mean?

EFSA identified a lowest observed adverse effect level of 1 mg of glycoalkaloids per kilogram of body weight per day. A 70 kg adult would reach the same dose-per-body-weight at 70 mg, while a 20 kg child would reach it at 20 mg. This is not a recommended intake or a home safety threshold; it simply illustrates why body size matters when exposure is considered.

Greening and sprouting are related but not identical

Light primarily drives greening, while age and storage conditions can encourage sprouting. A potato can be green without long sprouts, or sprouted without obvious green tissue. When both appear together—especially with softness or shriveling—the case for discarding becomes stronger.

Preventing green potatoes

Keep potatoes protected from light, including strong kitchen lighting and sunny counters. A dark, dry, well-ventilated storage place is better than a transparent bowl left in daylight. Buy amounts that can be used before quality deteriorates.

Bottom line

The green color itself is harmless chlorophyll, but it is a useful warning that the potato has been exposed to conditions that can also increase glycoalkaloids. Because the concentration cannot be judged from color and cooking reductions are highly variable, a clearly green potato is better discarded than “rescued” by peeling or frying.

Frequently asked questions

Is the green part solanine?

No. It is chlorophyll, but it can indicate conditions that also raise glycoalkaloids.

Can peeling make a green potato safe?

Peeling reduces glycoalkaloids but does not let you know the remaining amount; EFSA consumer guidance says not to eat green potatoes.

Does frying destroy solanine?

It can reduce glycoalkaloids variably, but not with enough predictability to rescue a clearly green potato.

faq.question: Is green potato color itself toxic?
faq.answer: No. The green is chlorophyll, but it signals light exposure that can coincide with increased glycoalkaloids.

faq.question: Should green potatoes be eaten after peeling?
faq.answer: EFSA consumer guidance advises against eating green potatoes.

faq.question: Can cooking make a green potato safe?
faq.answer: Processing can reduce glycoalkaloids but the reduction is variable and not a reliable home safety guarantee.
